propositions.text: This is an application for judicial review of the Officer's December 17, 2014 decision rejecting the Applicant's in-land permanent residence application on H&C grounds.
propositions.quote: This is an application for judicial review of the decision of an Immigration Officer (Officer), dated December 17, 2014, rejecting the Applicant’s in-land permanent residence application on humanitarian and compassionate (H&C) grounds made pursuant to section 25 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 (the Act).

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review of the Officer's December 17, 2014 decision rejecting the Applicant's in-land permanent residence application on H&C grounds.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is allowed.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, the application is allowed.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the application for judicial review.

propositions.text: The Applicant is an 82-year-old Israeli citizen who came to Canada on July 7, 2010, and has remained on a temporary visa.
propositions.quote: The Applicant is an 82 year-old citizen of Israel. In July 2010, the Applicant’s two daughters and their respective families immigrated to Canada. The Applicant came to Canada on July 7, 2010 and has remained in Canada on a temporary visa.

propositions.text: The Applicant applied for permanent residence under the parent and grandparent sponsorship program on January 3, 2014, after the program's temporary suspension was lifted.
propositions.quote: The Applicant applied for permanent residence under the parent and grandparent sponsorship program on January 3, 2014, two days after the temporary suspension was lifted on the program.

propositions.text: The Applicant's sponsorship application has been accepted for processing.
propositions.quote: Her application has since been accepted for processing.

propositions.text: On May 14, 2014, the Applicant applied for an exemption from in-Canada eligibility criteria to remain while the sponsorship application is processed.
propositions.quote: On May 14, 2014, the Applicant applied for an exemption from the in-Canada eligibility criteria, asking Citizenship and Immigration Canada (CIC) to allow her to remain in Canada while the sponsorship application is processed.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant is an 82-year-old Israeli citizen who came to Canada in 2010, applied for permanent residence in 2014, and sought an exemption to remain in Canada.

propositions.text: The Officer accepted the Applicant lives with a daughter, shares close family bonds, and is financially supported by her daughters and sons-in-law.
propositions.quote: The Officer accepted that the Applicant lives with one of her daughters in Canada, that she shares a close bond with all her family members in Canada, and that she is financially supported by her daughters and sons-in-law.

propositions.text: The Officer noted the Applicant's anxiety and depression over possible separation, with anti-anxiety medication use.
propositions.quote: The Officer also noted the Applicant’s anxiety and depression over the prospect of being separated from her family members in Canada as she is currently taking anti-anxiety medication.

propositions.text: The Officer found family dependency difficulties insufficient for H&C exemption, reasoning separation was expected as daughters chose to immigrate.
propositions.quote: In concluding that the difficulties related to family dependency were insufficient to justify an exemption on H&C grounds, the Officer found that while it would be difficult for the Applicant to leave Canada, the Applicant’s physical separation from her daughters was to be expected since the daughters decided to immigrate to Canada.

propositions.text: The Officer found the Applicant could endure separation, having been separated before, and maintain relationships through correspondence.
propositions.quote: The officer also found that the Applicant would be able to endure the separation as she was separated from her children in the past, that the separation would not be permanent, and that the Applicant would be able to continue her close relationship with her daughters and grandchildren through correspondence.

propositions.text: The Officer found the family would continue financial support if the Applicant returned to Israel.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the Officer found that her family would continue to support her financially if she were to return to Israel.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer found the Applicant lives with family, has anxiety, but separation was expected and manageable, with ongoing financial support if she returned to Israel.

propositions.text: The Officer failed to consider the disproportionate hardship aspect of the H&C test per the IP 5 Guidelines, despite evidence showing hardship if returned to Israel.
propositions.quote: The Applicant alleges that the Officer did not consider the disproportionate hardship aspect of the test as set out in the CIC Operational Manual, IP 5 – Immigrant Applications in Canada made on Humanitarian or Compassionate Grounds (IP 5 Guidelines) since the evidence submitted before the Officer clearly demonstrates that the Applicant would suffer a disproportionate hardship if she were to return to Israel.

propositions.text: The Applicant relies on Kaur to argue the Officer failed to address her personal circumstances.
propositions.quote: The Applicant also relies on Kaur v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 805 [Kaur] to argue that the Officer failed to address the Applicant’s personal circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the Officer failed to consider disproportionate hardship per IP 5 Guidelines and personal circumstances per Kaur.

propositions.text: The Officer erred in assessing physical separation hardship by not properly considering Applicant's age, dependency, and difficult life history.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the Officer erred in the assessment of physical separation as hardship since the Applicant’s age, high degree of dependency on her family, and difficult life were not properly considered.

propositions.text: Applicant lived in an orphanage for 12 years after abandonment, reunited with mother at 16, and endured an abusive marriage for children's sake.
propositions.quote: The Applicant states that she was forced to live in an orphanage for 12 years when her father abandoned her and attempted to cut the Applicant’s ties with her mother. The Applicant only reunited with her mother at the age of 16 after her mother remarried. At the young age of 19, the Applicant married a man 30 years her senior who was emotionally and physically abusive towards her, yet she remained in the marriage to care for her children.

propositions.text: The Officer's reliance on past separation to justify no undue hardship now at age 82 is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: While the Officer found that the Applicant was able to keep close contact with her daughters over 25 years ago while they were studying abroad, the Officer’s reliance on this point to justify that the Applicant would not suffer an undue, undeserved, and disproportionate hardship if she were to be physically separated from her family now at the age of 82 is unreasonable.

propositions.text: The Applicant relies on Nicayenzi to argue the Officer made speculative findings ignoring evidence of no relatives in Israel and daily dependency on Canadian family.
propositions.quote: The Applicant relies on Nicayenzi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 595, 457 FTR 65 [Nicayenzi] to argue that the Officer made findings of fact based on mere speculation in this regard since the evidence submitted demonstrates that the Applicant has no living relatives in Israel and significantly depends on her family in Canada to support and care for her socially, financially, and psychologically, on a daily basis.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the Officer erred by not properly considering her age, dependency, difficult life, and wrongly relied on past separation to deny hardship.

propositions.text: The Applicant challenges the Officer's finding that her psychiatrist's assessment was prepared as an advocate.
propositions.quote: The Applicant also challenges the Officer’s finding that the assessment prepared by her psychiatrist, Dr. Brotman, was prepared as an advocate for the Applicant.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant challenges the Officer's finding that her psychiatrist's assessment was advocacy.

propositions.text: The issue is whether the Officer committed a reviewable error by failing to consider disproportionate impact due to Applicant's personal circumstances.
propositions.quote: The issue raised by this judicial review application is whether the Officer, in concluding as he did, committed a reviewable error as contemplated by section 18.1(4) of the Federal Courts Act, RSC, 1985, c F-7, in failing to consider whether requiring the Applicant to return to Israel would have a disproportionate impact due to her personal circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The court frames the issue as whether the Officer erred by not considering disproportionate impact from Applicant's personal circumstances.

propositions.text: The standard of review is reasonableness for mixed fact and law questions in immigration officer decisions.
propositions.quote: The appropriate standard of review is reasonableness since the matter is related to the Officer’s assessment of mix questions of fact and law (New Brunswick (Board of Management) v Dunsmuir, 2008 SCC 9, [2008] 1 SCR 190, at para 47 [Dunsmuir]; Nicayenzi, above at para 10, Baker v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 SCR 817, [1999] SCJ No 39; Walker v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 447 at para 31, [2012] FCJ No 479 (QL); Kisana v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2009 FCA 189 at para 18, [2009] FCJ No 713).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the standard of review is reasonableness for mixed fact and law questions in immigration decisions.

propositions.text: Foreign nationals must apply for permanent residence outside Canada unless exempted for H&C reasons under section 25 of the Act.
propositions.quote: Generally, a foreign national must apply for a permanent resident visa from outside Canada. In order to be exempt from this requirement, the foreign national must demonstrate that the exemption is justified by H&C considerations relating to him or her pursuant to section 25 of the Act.

propositions.text: IP 5 Guidelines state H&C grounds may exist where applying from outside Canada would unreasonably impact the applicant due to personal circumstances.
propositions.quote: In this respect, the IP 5 Guidelines provide that H&C grounds may exist where the hardship of having to apply from outside Canada “would have an unreasonable impact on the applicant due to their personal circumstances.”

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the legal framework for H&C exemptions and the IP 5 Guidelines on personal circumstances hardship.

propositions.text: The Officer failed to properly address the Applicant's personal circumstances, especially her age and dependency on family in Canada.
propositions.quote: Upon review of the Officer's decision and the evidence before him, I am of the view that the Officer failed to properly address the Applicant's personal circumstances, particularly, the Applicant’s age and dependency on her family in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer failed to properly address the Applicant's personal circumstances, especially age and family dependency.

propositions.text: The Officer mentioned emotional support from family but did not thoroughly analyze this factor, constituting a reviewable error.
propositions.quote: While the Officer mentions in the summary section of his analysis that the family provides the Applicant with emotional support, he does not conduct a thorough analysis of this factor. In my view, and for the reasons that follow, this is a reviewable error.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer mentioned but did not thoroughly analyze emotional support, a reviewable error.

propositions.text: Immigration officers have discretion on weight of personal circumstances but cannot disregard them (Kaur, Koromila).
propositions.quote: This Court has held that while immigration officers have discretion as to the weight assigned to an applicant’s personal circumstances in H&C applications, officers cannot have any disregard for them. (Kaur, above at paras 18-19; Koromila v Canada (Citizenship and Immigrations), 2009 FC 393, at para 68 [Koromila]).

propositions.text: Officers cannot ignore significant evidence of emotional and human dependency on family, especially after fundamental personal changes (Le Blanc).
propositions.quote: This Court has also held that an immigration officer cannot ignore “significant evidence of an applicant’s emotional and human dependency on her family in Canada” (Koromila, above at para 68). This is especially true where a fundamental change has occurred in an applicant’s personal situation (Le Blanc v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 1292, at para 31[Le Blanc]).

paragraphs.summary: The court states officers have discretion but cannot disregard significant emotional dependency or fundamental personal changes.

propositions.text: The Officer found the daughters expected separation when immigrating to Canada and anticipated difficulties for the Applicant living alone in Israel.
propositions.quote: In response to the Applicant’s pleas, the Officer found that: […] when Ms. Epstein’s daughters applied to immigrate to Canada with their families, a separation would have been expected by them. In making the choice to leave Israel to live permanently in Canada, I find that Ms. Epstein’s daughters would have reasonably anticipated the difficulties that their mother would face living in Israel on her own with no family or friends.

paragraphs.summary: The court reports the Officer found the daughters expected separation and anticipated difficulties for the Applicant living alone in Israel.

propositions.text: The Officer failed to grasp the essential point: the Applicant's plea to remain with family in Canada in her final life stage.
propositions.quote: In my view, the Officer’s finding demonstrates that he failed to grasp the essential point of the application. The H&C application is the plea of an elderly woman to remain with her family in Canada as she waits for her permanent residency application to be processed.

propositions.text: Applicant's daughters postponed immigration to stay with her in Israel to keep family together.
propositions.quote: Indeed, her daughters postponed their immigration to Canada for several years to be with the Applicant in Israel in order to keep the family together.

propositions.text: Applicant is dependent on family in Canada for shelter, food, emotional and financial support, relying entirely on them for daily needs.
propositions.quote: The evidence is clear that the Applicant is dependent on her family in Canada to provide her with shelter, food, and emotional and financial support. In sum, the Applicant is entirely reliant on her family for her daily needs.

propositions.text: The Officer disregarded fundamental personal circumstances by omitting to consider Applicant's emotional and physical dependency, constituting reviewable errors.
propositions.quote: In omitting to consider the Applicant’s emotional and physical dependency on her family, the Officer disregarded personal circumstances of the Applicant that were fundamental to her claim. The Officer’s failure to properly assess the evidence and failure to have regard to relevant personal circumstances of the Applicant constitute reviewable errors (Aguirre v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 274, 450 FTR 301, at para 9; Kaur, above at para 18).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer failed to grasp the Applicant's plea to remain with family, disregarded her dependency, and made reviewable errors.

propositions.text: The Officer's finding that Applicant could maintain relationships through correspondence ignored her significant isolation if returned to Israel.
propositions.quote: Moreover, in concluding that the Applicant would be able to “maintain her close relationship with her daughters’ families through correspondence, telephone calls and visits when she returns to Israel.” In my view, by characterizing the facts in this manner, the Officer ignored the Applicant’s change in circumstances, namely, that she would be significantly isolated if she were to return to Israel.

propositions.text: Justice Shore in Yu stated living together differs significantly from occasional visits.
propositions.quote: As Justice Shore stated in Yu v Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration), 2006 FC 956, at paragraph 30, “[t]here is a significant factual difference between living together and sharing day-to-day life and an occasional visit.”

propositions.text: The Officer failed to grasp the difference between living together and occasional contact, ignoring the significant change in Applicant's personal circumstances.
propositions.quote: In this case, the Officer failed to grasp this difference when analyzing the personal circumstances of the Applicant. The family’s move to Canada is a significant change in the Applicant’s personal circumstances with respect to her emotional and personal support network as the evidence is clear that the Applicant’s close relationship with her family encompasses so much more than just occasional conversations over the phone or the occasional visit.

propositions.text: Significant change and advanced age impose a duty on the Officer to analyze personal circumstances more substantially (Le Blanc).
propositions.quote: This significant change, coupled with the advanced age of the Applicant, and evidence of significant isolation if she were to return to Israel, placed a duty on the Officer to carry out a more substantial analysis of the Applicant’s significant change in personal circumstances (Le Blanc v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 1292, at para 31).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer ignored the Applicant's significant isolation and failed to analyze the difference between living together and occasional contact, breaching duty.

propositions.text: The Officer's decision is unreasonable and outside acceptable outcomes; no need to decide on psychiatrist's assessment weight.
propositions.quote: In my opinion, the Officer’s decision does not fall within a range of possible, acceptable outcomes, defensible in fact and in law. Given this finding, there is no need to determine whether the Officer unreasonably gave no weight to the assessment prepared by the Applicant’s psychiatrist.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the Officer's decision is unreasonable and does not fall within acceptable outcomes, so no need to assess psychiatrist's report weight.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is allowed, the matter is referred back to CIC for redetermination by a different officer, and no question is certified.
propositions.quote: THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that: 1. The application for judicial review is allowed; 2. The matter is referred back to Citizenship and Immigration Canada to be redetermined by a different immigration officer; and 3. No question is certified.

paragraphs.summary: The court orders the application allowed, matter referred back for redetermination by a different officer, and no question certified.
